articles.text:
DEEPFAKES TARGETING women during state elections, a rise in scam content using Al, better enforcement rather than new laws, and lack of uniform definition for "deepfake" - these are some of the key concerns raised by stakeholders, according to a status report submitted by the Ministry of Electronics and Information

Technology (MeitY) to the Delhi High Court on Monday. According to the report, a nine-member committee set up by MeitYin November 2024 met a month later. The committee then met technology and policy stakeholders on January 21 this year. The stakeholders pressed for mandatory regulation around Al content disclosure with a caveat that the emphasis should be on malicious actors rather than on creative uses of

deepfake technology. The minutes of the meetings, made part of the status report, notes that various stakeholders in attendance emphasised that "...there should be regulation around mandatory Al content disclosure, labeling standards, and grievance redressal mechanisms, while giving emphasison malicious actors rather than benign or creative uses of deepfake technology".

THERE IS realisation among stakeholders that deepfakes need to be tackled, and through increased oversight on malicious actors. The minutes suggest companies cannot shy away from taking any liability.

J&K Chief Minister Omar Abdullah at the IndiraGandhi Memorial Tulip Garden in Srinagar after it was opened to the public on Wednesday. The 50-hectare tulip garden is Asia's largest. ANI

and girls glue sequins on
shararas and kurtas in the by-
lanes of Bapunagar, a labour
colony in Surat’s Pandesara in-
dustrial area.

Five years ago, these lanes,
home totrained migrant workers
who form the backboneof Surat’s

dyeing, printing, powerloom and
embroidery units, were nearly

It was a walk like none other.

modes of transport and urging
people to stay indoors — to check
the spread of the rampaging
Covid-19 virus, at labour hubs
across the country, from Surat to
Kolkata, Chennai to Gurgaon,
migrant workers trudged hun-
dreds of kilometres back to their
homes in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar,
Jharkhand, Odisha, Maharashtra,
Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.

Among those who walked
then was Ramanand Paswan, 35,
atextile factory worker in Surat.
Around three months after the
lockdown, with no workand his
savings drying up, Ramanand
had decided to go back to his
family in Gongara, a village in
Bihar’s Aurangabad district
nearly 2,000 km from Surat.
Five years later, now back
where he began that night, he
says, “We were 10 ofus, ali from
different villages in Aurangabad.
People were dying all around us
and I thought, if I have to die, I
would rather die at home, with
my family around me. When | fi-
nally left, | had Rs 100 in my
pocket. Icarried a water bottle, a

few packets of biscuits, my mo-
bile phone and charger, and
three pairs of clothes.”
With a nationwide curfew in
place, Ramanand and his friends
decided to walk at night, when
the police weren't looking — or
when they looked away.
From Surat, the group walked
to Nandurbar in Maharashtra,
then crossed over into Madhya
Pradesh. “Somewhere at the
Maharashtra-Madhya Pradesh
border, we stopped a truck and
got a ride for 10 kilometres. After
that, we continued our walk. We
would start walking early in the
morning, stop at noon, rest tillthe
sun went down, and start walk-
ing again. Itwaseasier to walk at

night. Sometimes, we would stop
at one of the villages and if we
were lucky, we would get some
food, There were many nights
and days when we only had wa-
ter,” he says, sitting on a plastic
chair in Bapunagar. Hedoesn’t re-
member the number of days he
walked — “over a month, I think”.

Bapunagar and even the same
roommates,
Six months ago, he moved
his wife Sandhya, 32, and their
two children to Surat. “The chil-
dren study at a local municipal

school. Sandhya also makes
some money sticking sequins on
readymade clothes. Unlike Surat,
we haveno other means of liveli-
hood back home in Bihar. This is
why] decided to shift my family
here,” says Ramanand, who
earns Rs 20,000 a month.

work in units in the Pandesara
and Sachin areas of Surat, which
is among the largest textile pro-
ducersin the country. Pandesara
and nearby areas such as Vadod
have undergone drastic changes
since the pandemic, say its resi-
dents. The dusty roads have
